title: God’s Sovereignty and Alexander the Great
speaker: Dr. Battle

outline.title: The Sovereignty of God in History
subpoints: God uses historical events for His purposes
Comfort in knowing God controls history despite chaos
Alexander the Great as an instrument of divine will

outline.title: Fulfillment of Prophecy: The Destruction of Tyre
subpoints: Ezekiel 26 predicts the scraping away of Tyre's rubble
Alexander’s construction of a causeway to the island
Literal fulfillment of the prophecy centuries later

outline.title: Daniel’s Prophecies of the Greek Empire
subpoints: Daniel 2: The bronze section of Nebuchadnezzar’s statue
Daniel 7: The four-winged leopard representing Greece
Daniel 8: The goat with the prominent horn attacking the ram

outline.title: The Division of Alexander’s Kingdom
subpoints: The breaking of the large horn at the height of power
The four small horns representing the four generals
The rise of the Seleucid line

outline.title: Preparation for the Gospel
subpoints: Alexander’s conquests spread Greek culture and language
Preparation for the Greek New Testament
God’s purpose in using a pagan conqueror

summary:
This sermon explores the doctrine of divine sovereignty by examining how God used the historical figure of Alexander the Great to fulfill Old Testament prophecies and prepare the world for the spread of the Gospel. The speaker highlights that while human history often appears chaotic, God is actively directing events to further His redemptive plan. Alexander, though unaware of his role in biblical history, served as an instrument of God’s will, demonstrating that no power on earth operates outside of divine oversight.

The teaching focuses on specific prophetic passages in Ezekiel and Daniel that were written centuries before Alexander’s rise. Ezekiel 26 is cited as a literal prophecy regarding the destruction of the city of Tyre, which Alexander fulfilled by constructing a causeway to the island and reducing the city to a bare rock. In Daniel, the Greek Empire is identified through various symbols, including the bronze section of Nebuchadnezzar’s statue, the four-winged leopard, and the goat with a prominent horn. These prophecies accurately describe Alexander’s rapid conquests and the subsequent division of his empire into four parts after his death.

Ultimately, the sermon emphasizes that Alexander’s legacy was not merely military but theological. By unifying the known world under Greek culture and language, he inadvertently prepared the stage for the apostles to spread the New Testament message throughout the Mediterranean. This perspective offers comfort to believers, reminding them that even in times of turmoil and political upheaval, God remains in control, using all of history to bring about His eternal purposes.
